📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

Former Ethereum Foundation developer Trent Van Epps warns that Ethereum could face a funding crisis within the next 3–9 months 

For years, the Ethereum Foundation has followed a “subtraction” strategy—gradually reducing its influence so the network can thrive independently. However, EF still remains a key pillar of legitimacy through its brand, ties to Vitalik Buterin, developer events, and ecosystem coordination.

The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it.

Trump Turns Housing Bill Into Hostage

Donald Trump just discovered a new way to do “art of the deal”: hold a bipartisan housing bill hostage until the Senate swears loyalty to his election‑rules crusade. 

An hour and a half before he was supposed to sign one of the only laws on affordability that actually polls well, he nuked his own ceremony on social media, declaring the event “hereby cancelled” until the Senate passes his “desperately needed” SAVE AMERICA ACT — which he grandly calls a “National Emergency.” 

The table, the chair, the cameras in Statuary Hall all stayed; only the signature didn’t show up.

On paper, the 21st Road to Housing Act is the kind of thing presidents beg to be photographed with in an election year: a bipartisan package to increase supply, cap Wall Street’s zombie landlord game at 350 single‑family homes per investor, rewrite mobile‑home rules, and pump federal grants into new building. 

Even Trump’s own team was busy selling it as “one of the most significant pieces of housing affordability legislation in American history,” a “signature commitment” from his State of the Union. 

Then he logged on, called it “of minor importance” and sneered that it was an “Elizabeth ‘Pocahontas’ Warren–centric housing bill.” His base heard the slur; the rest of the country heard: my voters’ rent crisis is leverage, not policy.

The Senate GOP is caught in the usual Trump triangle: they don’t have the votes for his SAVE AMERICA ACT, they do have the votes for the housing bill, and they just watched their own president blow up their one campaign talking point about helping “working families.” 

Rounds and Tillis sound like middle managers begging the CEO not to shoot the product on launch day: “We thought the president was behind it… apparently maybe not,” “we’ve got to get our act together and stop surprising people.” 

He’s tanking a win because he wants proof‑of‑citizenship rules, tighter mail voting, and a few anti‑trans culture‑war treats on his desk first — and if renters have to wait, that’s their problem.

The Democrats, of course, get to play the shocked adults. Schumer calls on Trump to “stop making such a fool of himself.” Warren reminds everyone that he’s called affordability concerns a “hoax” and now walks away from a bill she co‑wrote with Tim Scott, one of the few examples of actual cross‑party legislating left in Washington. 

Trump’s own allies, like Speaker Mike Johnson, try to explain the stunt as “just a delay” while openly admitting they’ll use the time to push the voting bill. 

The White House, asked if he’ll at least sign the housing bill quietly, simply replies with a screenshot of his Truth post — because nothing says functioning government like governing by meme.

Underneath the drama, the message is brutally simple. If Congress wants even “minor importance” policy on housing, it has to pay a toll in election‑law obedience. 

A law that bans mega‑landlords from hoarding neighborhoods suddenly becomes bargaining chip number 37 in a long fight over who gets to vote, how, and with which identity documents.

Landlords, institutional investors and housing‑market speculators just got told: relax, your cap can wait, the president needs a better hostage first. Voters got told: your rent and mortgage are now campaign collateral.

So the “affordable housing” photo op turns into yet another loyalty test. Trump can still let the bill become law without his signature, or send it back and dare Congress to override. 

In the meantime, everyone goes back to their usual roles: Republicans insisting they’re the party of families while shrugging as the president torpedoes their own bill, Democrats pretending principle while quietly enjoying the show, and millions of renters watching Washington prove — again — that in this system, even bipartisan crumbs can be pulled mid‑air if they’re not useful enough in the next power play.
